evidence_quote: On average, charter middle schools that hold lotteries are neither more nor less successful than traditional public schools in improving student achievement, behavior, and school progress; however, impacts varied widely across schools.
resolved_title: The Evaluation of Charter School Impacts (NCEE, 2010)
notes: Lottery sample of applicants to oversubscribed charter middle schools; abstract states no applicant eligibility rule beyond applying. Kraft n 2330, grades 4-7, not verifiable from the abstract. wwc-codes row 365 has no sample text.

evidence_quote: Results with 94 teachers and 416 students indicate that peer tutoring was more effective in increasing academic engagement of low-SES students than teacher instruction.
resolved_title: Longitudinal effects of classwide peer tutoring (Journal of Educational Psychology, 1989)
notes: Abstract reports a low versus high SES contrast as an analysis, not a sampling rule, and gives no eligibility statement; a classwide program suggests universal but the text does not say. Kraft n 416 matches the abstract.

evidence_quote: Specifically, if a charter school in New York receives more applicants than it has places, it must hold a random lottery among the applicants. Lotteries are specific to a school, grade, and year of intended entry
resolved_title: Charter Schools in New York City: Who Enrolls and How They Affect Their Students' Achievement (NBER Working Paper 14852, 2009)
notes: Lotteried-in versus lotteried-out applicants to NYC charter schools, tests in grades 3-8; no applicant eligibility rule beyond applying. Text is the NBER working paper. Kraft n 32551 not checked against the paper's tables.

evidence_quote: District selection was based upon factors such as district size and poverty ... The selected districts, which were spread across 13 states, served low-income students, with every district in the study having more than 50 percent of its students qualifying for the federal School Lunch Program.
resolved_title: Impacts of Comprehensive Teacher Induction: Results from the Second Year of a Randomized Controlled Study (NCEE 2009-4072)
notes: Districts chosen partly on poverty; within districts, all beginning K-6 teachers in the study schools and their students, no student rule. Kraft n 3000 does not match any report sample (one-year districts 1,917 reading and 1,683 math students, p. 34; two-year districts 1,303 and 1,242); possibly a sum or a rounded figure.

evidence_quote: Subjects: A total of 2,308 elementary students eligible for and interested in attending a 21st Century Community Learning Center. A total of 973 students applied to 18 centers in fall 2000, and 1,335 applied to 8 centers in fall 2001.
resolved_title: When Schools Stay Open Late: The National Evaluation of the 21st Century Community Learning Centers Program: Final Report (2005)
notes: Applicants to oversubscribed after-school centers were randomized (p. 34). Centers were chosen for oversubscription, and the report describes the program as serving mostly low-income schools, but no student selection rule beyond applying. Kraft n 2308 matches.

evidence_quote: This reports focuses on a sample of 1,764 students (referred to in this report as the study sample) who applied for one of the Career Academies selected for the study.
resolved_title: Career Academies: Impacts on Students' Engagement and Performance in High School (MDRC, 2000)
notes: Lottery among applicants identified in grade 8 or 9. MDRC's interest in at-risk students (p. 19) is motivation, not a sample rule (tie-breaker 7). Kraft n 1764 matches the study sample, but the standardized achievement test was given to a 490-student subsample (p. 20), so Kraft's test-score effects likely rest on that subsample, hence mixed_samples 1. wwc-codes row describes a 1,482-student grade 9-12 sample.

evidence_quote: The effects of a voluntary summer reading intervention were assessed in a randomized field trial involving 552 students in 10 schools. In this study, fourth-grade children received eight books to read during their summer vacation
resolved_title: Effects of a Voluntary Summer Reading Intervention on Reading Achievement: Results From a Randomized Field Trial (EEPA, 2006)
notes: Voluntary describes the summer reading, not enrollment; fourth graders in 10 schools with no student rule stated. Subgroup effects reported for Black, Latino, and less fluent readers, but Kraft's 0.01 is consistent with an overall effect. Kraft n 552 matches.

evidence_quote: The causal effects of a voluntary summer reading intervention on children's reading activities and reading achievement were assessed in a randomized experiment involving 331 children in Grades 1-5.
resolved_title: The effects of a voluntary summer reading intervention on reading activities and reading achievement (Journal of Educational Psychology, 2007, 99(3), 505-515)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: the abstract (ERIC EJ772024, DOI 10.1037/0022-0663.99.3.505) is the correct article, Kim 2007, and Kraft's n 331 matches; no open full text was found. The abstract states no school or student eligibility rule: children were pretested, stratified by grade and classroom, and randomized to receive 10 matched books over the summer. The word voluntary describes the summer reading, not enrollment, and nothing describes an application, so opt_in 0. Because the abstract does not say whether all children in the participating classrooms took part or how the site was chosen, the code is unclear rather than universal.

evidence_quote: To be eligible for a scholarship, children had to be entering grades one through five, living in New York City, attending a public school at the time of application, and be a member of a family with an income that qualified children for the federal School Lunch Program.
resolved_title: School Choice in New York City After Three Years: An Evaluation of the School Choice Scholarships Program: Final Report (Mathematica, 2002)
notes: Income-eligible applicants randomized by lottery. 85 percent of scholarships were reserved for applicants from public schools with below-median test scores (p. 12); that is a school-level performance weight in the lottery, not an eligibility rule, and estimates are weighted back to all eligible applicants. Kraft n 1960 not verified in text.

evidence_quote: Analyzes the impact of a negative income tax experiment on the school performance of children in grades 4 through 10
resolved_title: The Effects of a Negative Income Tax on School Performance: Results of an Experiment (Journal of Human Resources, 1979)
notes: Abstract gives no eligibility rule. Families in a negative income tax experiment are enrolled by income, which would make this targeted_other at the family level with opt_in 1 if the full text confirms it. Kraft n 851 not verifiable.

evidence_quote: is more effective than current science programs in five diverse sites--Federal Way Public Schools (Washington), Ogden City School District (Utah), Reynodsburg City Schools (Ohio), St. Petersburg Catholic Schools (Florida), and Visalia Unified School District (California).
resolved_title: Comparative Effectiveness of Scott Foresman Science: A Report of Randomized Experiments in Five School Districts (Empirical Education, 2007)
notes: Whole-class curriculum comparison with teachers and students in five districts; the abstract states no student or school need criterion, so universal is inferred from the design rather than stated, hence low. A reviewer may prefer unclear. Kraft n 2638 and grades 3-5 not verifiable; reading 0.05 is a secondary outcome.

evidence_quote: Schools were eligible for selection into the study if they met two criteria: Program criterion. At least 80 percent of the mathematics and science teachers signed the application form indicating that they wanted to participate in AMSTI. ... Study criterion. The school housed at least one of grades 4-8.
resolved_title: Evaluation of the Effectiveness of the Alabama Math, Science, and Technology Initiative (AMSTI). Final Report (NCEE 2012-4008)
notes: Schools applied to the state program and were selected to resemble regional populations (p. 42); no need-based rule at school or student level (tie-breaker 6). Kraft n 780 is the report's approximate teacher count, not students (about 30,000 students eligible; reading analytic sample 7,528 students in 79 schools, p. 27). Study-list key 633-dumont-2012 and author fields (dumont, trautwein, ludtke) do not match the citation Newman et al. 2012; looks like a study-list error.

evidence_quote: This randomized field experiment was designed to gauge program impacts on the reading achievement of 978 urban students in Grades 3 to 6. Schools and teachers within schools volunteered to participate in the study
resolved_title: A Randomized Experimental Evaluation of the Impact of Accelerated Reader/Reading Renaissance Implementation on Reading Achievement in Grades 3 to 6 (JESPAR, 2006)
notes: Schools and teachers volunteered (tie-breaker 6); no student rule. Kraft n 1023 does not match the abstract's 978 students.

evidence_quote: random assignment of 364 second through sixth grade students to classrooms and random assignment of participating classrooms to control and experimental groups was implemented in a school district located in East Texas.
resolved_title: The Effects of Brain Gym as a General Education Intervention: Improving Academic Performance and Behaviors (dissertation, 2010)
notes: Class-wide tier-one intervention for all students. The only achievement results in the abstract are for the at-risk subgroup (t(66) and t(71), roughly 70 students), so Kraft's reading and math effects may come from that subgroup while n 364 is the full sample; mixed_samples 1.

evidence_quote: Researchers randomly assigned 67 elementary schools to receive CASL materials or continue with regularly scheduled professional development. ... Analysis of all schools and 9,596 students failed to yield statistically significant impacts of CASL on student mathematics achievement
resolved_title: Impacts of professional development in classroom assessment on teacher and student outcomes (Journal of Educational Research, DOI 10.1080/00220671.2014.992581)
notes: Abstract is the journal version of the 2011 REL Central report Kraft cites. Whole-school professional development; no student rule. Kraft n 4700 does not match the 9,596 students in the abstract (possibly grade 4 only or one cohort).

evidence_quote: Students and teachers were randomly assigned to either the SEM-R treatment with 1 hr of SEMR and 1 hr of basal instruction or to the control group with 2 hr of basal instruction.
resolved_title: Using Enrichment Reading Practices to Increase Reading Fluency, Comprehension, and Attitudes (Journal of Educational Research, 2008)
notes: Schoolwide enrichment model delivered to whole classes in grades 3-5; abstract gives no site description or sample size, so Kraft's n 558 cannot be checked and universal is inferred from the design rather than stated.

evidence_quote: Family Rewards was targeted toward families who lived in selected community districts and who had incomes at or below 130 percent of the federal poverty level. Eligible families had to have at least one child in the fourth, seventh, or ninth grade.
resolved_title: Toward Reduced Poverty Across Generations: Early Findings from New York City's Conditional Cash Transfer Program (MDRC, 2010)
notes: Family-level income and residence rule in six high-poverty community districts; families volunteered and were randomized by lottery. Level coded student because the rule is the family's income, not the school's. Kraft n 11311 is close to the report's about 11,000 children. wwc-codes row matched Miller and Riccio (2011), an SREE paper on the same trial.

evidence_quote: We examine how employers learn about worker productivity in a randomized pilot experiment which provided objective estimates of teacher performance to school principals.
resolved_title: Information and Employee Evaluation: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in Public Schools (AER, 2012)
notes: Abstract describes a school-level information treatment to principals and says nothing about which schools or students were in the sample; likely universal within participating schools but not stated. Kraft n 1434 not verifiable.

evidence_quote: Only students whose family income was at or below 1.75 times the national poverty line were eligible to apply.
resolved_title: Private School Vouchers and Student Achievement: An Evaluation of the Milwaukee Parental Choice Program (NBER Working Paper 5964, 1997 version of the 1998 QJE article)
notes: Income-eligible applicants, random selection at oversubscribed choice schools. Analysis sample is African-American and Hispanic applicants in grades K-8, 1990-1993 (p. 11). Kraft n 2258 is close to the approximately 2,300 applicants with data (p. 18).

evidence_quote: Of the 12 public elementary schools that agreed to participate in a randomized study of physical education, 7 were selected for the study. ... Informed consent was obtained from 98% of fourth grade students and their parents.
resolved_title: Effects of Health-Related Physical Education on Academic Achievement: SPARK (Research Quarterly for Exercise and Sport, 1999)
notes: Whole-school PE program in a relatively affluent suburban district; consent was for measurement, not for program entry, so opt_in 0. Kraft n 759 matches the achievement test sample. Kraft lists three effects for two subjects; the paper analyzes two cohorts separately (test samples 330 and 424).

evidence_quote: Program eligibility requirements included residing in a targeted development, having very low income that met the Section 8 income limits of the public housing authority, having a child under eighteen, and being in good standing with the housing authority.
resolved_title: Neighborhoods and Academic Achievement: Results from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment (NBER Working Paper 11909, 2006)
notes: Families in public housing in tracts with 40 percent or higher poverty who volunteered for MTO and were assigned by lottery; child sample ages 6 to 20 tested in 2002. Level coded student because the rule is the family's. Kraft n 5074 and three effects for two subjects not checked against tables.

evidence_quote: Achievement and attitudinal effects of three mathematics instruction methods directed in varying degrees toward accommodating diversity in student performance levels were compared in two randomized field experiments.
resolved_title: Effects of Whole Class, Ability Grouped, and Individualized Instruction on Mathematics Achievement (AERJ 22(3), 1985)
notes: Abstract names no site or sample; whole-class instructional methods imply no student selection but the text does not say. Kraft n 480 (22 classrooms per Fryer's table) not verifiable. wwc-codes citation reads 1984, 12(4), 725-736, which does not match AERJ 22(3) 1985.

evidence_quote: Middle school teachers of mathematics were eligible to participate. A teacher could give instruction in other subjects but needed to teach at least ten students who would take the state's annual mathematics assessment in the spring in order to remain eligible. ... As noted, only volunteers were included in the experiment.
resolved_title: POINT/CounterPOINT: The View from the Trenches of Education Policy Research (Ballou, Springer, McCaffrey, Lockwood, Stecher, Hamilton, Pepper; Education Finance and Policy 7(2), 2012)
notes: Text file is the companion article on the POINT experiment, not the Springer et al. 2010 final report Kraft cites, hence medium. Selection was teacher volunteering in Nashville middle schools; no student rule. Kraft grades 5-8 and n 23784 not verifiable here.

evidence_quote: The study includes teachers on 78 teams of teachers teaching core subjects to students in grades 6 to 8 in nine middle schools. These are all the teams in the schools.
resolved_title: Team Pay for Performance: Experimental Evidence from Round Rock's Project on Incentives in Teaching (SREE 2011 conference abstract; McCaffrey, Pane, Springer, Burns, Haas)
notes: Text is an 8-page SREE conference abstract of the Round Rock team-incentive trial, not the 2012 report, hence medium. All teams in all nine district middle schools; no student rule. Kraft n 17383 not verifiable here.

evidence_quote: each of 13 KIPP schools used a lottery to randomly assign students either to receive an offer to attend the KIPP school or to not receive an offer.
resolved_title: KIPP Middle Schools: Impacts on Achievement and Other Outcomes, Final Report (Mathematica, 2013), as summarized by the WWC
notes: abstracts/923-tuttle-2013.txt is the Education Finance and Policy article (DOI 10.1162/edfp_a_00119) reporting the propensity-score analysis of 41 schools, not the lottery experiment Kraft's effects come from, so it was not used. WWC lottery sample: 725 students on state tests and 1,016 on TerraNova, the latter close to Kraft's n 1000; entry grades 5 and 6.

evidence_quote: All students from low-income families entering a grade between kindergarten and twelfth grade were eligible. PACE offered scholarships to 515 students who were in public schools at the time and 250 students who were already enrolled in private schools.
resolved_title: School Choice in Dayton, Ohio after Two Years: An Evaluation of the Parents Advancing Choice in Education Scholarship Program (2001)
notes: Income-eligible applicants, scholarships by lottery. Kraft n 515 matches the public-school scholarship count. Study-list key 985-mitchem-2001 and author fields (mitchem young west) do not match the citation West et al. 2001; flag for the study list.

evidence_quote: The study included fourth- and fifth-grade classrooms from 45 rural and suburban elementary schools, 12 school districts, and two states in the United States.
resolved_title: Large-scale randomized controlled trial with 4th graders using intelligent tutoring of the structure strategy (ETR&D 2012)
notes: recoded after re-retrieval 2026-09-18: the article is paywalled and no abstract was returned, so the code rests on the WWC study page per codebook section 5 step 3: whole fourth- and fifth-grade classrooms in 45 schools with no stated eligibility rule; twin rows 997 and 1000 coded identically.

evidence_quote: Because the program was oversubscribed in its early years of operation, and vouchers were awarded by lottery, we were able to use the gold standard evaluation method of a randomized experiment
resolved_title: School Vouchers and Student Outcomes: Experimental Evidence from Washington, DC (JPAM, 2013)
notes: Abstract is the 2013 journal article, not the 2010 final report Kraft cites. It states the lottery among applicants but not the applicant eligibility rule; if OSP eligibility was income-based, as the report would state, the code is targeted_other with level student. opt_in 1 because families applied. Kraft n 2300, grades K-12, not verifiable.
